# THE RANDOM SUBSEQUENCE MODEL AND UNIFORM CODES FOR THE DELETION CHANNEL

Abstract. We introduce the _Random Subsequence Model_, a spin glass model on pairs of random strings \((X,Y)\in\{0,1\}^N\times\{0,1\}^M\) whose partition function counts subsequence embeddings of _Y_ into _X_. We study two variants: the null model, where _X_ and _Y_ are independent and uniform, and the planted model, where _X_ is uniform and _Y_ is a uniformly-random length-_M_ subsequence of _X_. We connect the Random Sub- sequence Model to longstanding problems in various fields, including the best rate achievable by uniformly- random codes in the deletion channel, the longest common subsequence problem between two random strings, and models of directed polymers in statistical physics.

In the regime where \(N,M\rightarrow\infty\) at a fixed ratio \(\alpha=M/N\in(0,1)\), we exhibit strict asymptotic separations between the null annealed free energy and the quenched free energies of the null and planted models at all values of the density parameter \(\alpha\). This suggests that these models are in a spin glass phase at zero temperature throughout the entire dense regime. As a consequence, we show that uniformly-random codes achieve a positive rate in the deletion channel for all deletion probabilities \(p\in[0,1)\), settling multiple conjectures of [PIW24] and proving the first such positive rate result for the regime \(p\ge 1/2\).

We also give an exact analytic formula for the annealed free energy of the planted model for all values of the density parameter. This implies a corresponding analytic upper bound on the best rate achievable by uniformly-random codes in the deletion channel, complementing the lower bound from our first result. Our upper and lower bounds for the capacity of the deletion channel under uniform codes are far closer to each other than the best known upper and lower bounds for the capacity of the deletion channel.

### 1. Introduction

This paper introduces and studies the _Random Subsequence Model_, a new spin glass model whose zero- temperature partition function counts order-preserving subsequence embeddings for pairs of random binary strings. Given natural numbers \(M\le N\), the _configuration space_ of the model is

\(\Sigma=\Sigma_{N,M}:=\left\{\sigma:[M]\rightarrow[N]:\sigma\text{is strictly increasing}\right\}.\)

Given a pair of random strings \((X,Y)\in\{0,1\}^N\times\{0,1\}^M\), which we call the _disorder_, the _partition function_ is defined as

(1.1) \(Z_{X,Y}:=|S_{X,Y}|:=|\{\sigma\in\Sigma:X_\sigma=Y\}|,\)

where, for a configuration \(\sigma\in\Sigma\), we write

\(X_\sigma=\left(X_{\sigma(1)},\dots,X_{\sigma(M)}\right)\in\{0,1\}^M.\)

In words, _Z<sub>X,Y</sub>_ counts the number of order-preserving embeddings of _Y_ into _X_ as a subsequence. Fixing a density parameter \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), we are interested in the asymptotic regime in which \(N,M\rightarrow\infty\) with \(M/N\rightarrow\alpha\in[0,1]\) under two natural laws on the disorder.

**Null.** _X_ and _Y_ are drawn independently and uniformly from {0,1}_<sup>N</sup>_ and {0,1}_<sup>M</sup>_, respectively.

**Planted.** _X_ is drawn uniformly from {0,1}_<sup>N</sup>_, \(\sigma^*\) is drawn independently of _X_ and uniformly from \(\Sigma\), and we set \(Y=X_{\sigma^*}\).

## 1.1. Connections.

Before presenting our results, we connect the Random Subsequence Model to some longstanding problems in information theory, discrete probability, theoretical computer science, and statistical physics. The connections to problems in information theory are repeated here for the reader’s convenience from \[PIW24\], where the planted variant of the Random Subsequence Model was implicitly studied. For further such background, including connections to Slepian-Wolf theory and distributed storage, we refer the reader to the introduction of that paper.

### 1.1.1. _The deletion channel._

The _binary deletion channel with deletion probability_ \(p\in[0,1]\) is the communication channel which takes input \(x\in\{0,1\}^N\) and deletes each bit of _x_ independently with probability _p_ to produce a random output \(y\in\{0,1\}^*\). The deletion channel is often regarded as the canonical example of a channel with synchronization errors, that is, in which synchronization between input and output bit positions is lost. Dobrushin’s classical coding theorem for synchronization channels \[Dob67\] showed that the _capacity_ of the deletion channel, which can be thought of informally as the maximum rate at which one can reliably transmit information through the channel, admits the variational representation

\(lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} max_X\frac{1}{N}I\left(X;Y\right),\)

where the maximum is over all distributions of _X_ supported on {0,1}_<sup>N</sup>_, _Y_ is the output of the deletion channel on input _X_, and \(I(\cdot;\cdot)\) is the mutual information. Finding an analytic formula expressing the capacity above as a function of the deletion probability _p_ has been one of the outstanding problems of information theory over the past several decades.

A natural relaxation of the capacity problem is to consider _X_∼Unif{0,1}_<sup>N</sup>_ rather than optimizing over all possible laws of _X_. We refer to the corresponding limit

(1.2) \(lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}I\left(X;Y\right),X\sim\text{Unif}\{0,1\}^N\)

as the _uniform capacity_ of the deletion channel, which gives a lower bound on the full channel capacity, and can be interpreted as the maximum rate that can be achieved with _uniformly random error correcting codes_. Uniformly random codes are of substantial importance as they are known to be asymptotically optimal (i.e., they achieve the channel capacity) in many well-understood memoryless channels like the binary symmetric channel and the binary erasure channel (e.g., see \[Sha48\]), the latter of which is often thought of as the memoryless analogue of the binary deletion channel. As such, uniform codes are widely studied throughout information theory and coding theory. While it is known (e.g., see \[DSV12\] and \[DM06\]) that uniform codes cannot achieve the capacity of the deletion channel for _p_ close to 1, we believe that studying uniformly-random codes in this setting is both interesting in its own right and potentially an important stepping stone towards the full capacity problem, since deriving an analytic formula or even a convincing conjectural expression for (1.2) is wide open.

The uniform capacity of the deletion channel is closely connected to the planted variant of the Random Subsequence Model, and this connection is the primary motivation for the present work. Specifically, it is easy to show (see Appendix A) that, letting \(\alpha=1-p\), one can write

(1.3) \(lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}I(X;Y)=\alpha log2-h(\alpha)+lim_{N,M\rightarrow\infty M/N=\alpha}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\left[logZ_{X,Y}\right],\)

where all logs are taken base _e_ and

\(h(\alpha)=-\alpha log\alpha-(1-\alpha)log(1-\alpha)\)

<tbc>denotes the usual binary entropy function. Hence, understanding the _limiting free energy density_

\(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha):=\mathrm{lim}_{N,M\rightarrow\infty M/N=\alpha}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}Z_{X,Y}\right]\)

of this model is equivalent to computing the maximum rate achieved by uniformly random codes in the deletion channel.

Finally, we note that the null variant of the Random Subsequence Model is relevant to uniformly random codes for the deletion channel as well, and refer the reader to \[Mit09\] for additional discussion in this direction. Indeed, let \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{0,1\}^N\) be a uniformly-random code, with all elements of C drawn i.i.d. uniformly from {0,1}_<sup>N</sup>_. Let _X_∼C be a uniformly-random codeword and _Y_ the output of the deletion channel on input _X_. The maximum-likelihood decoder outputs<tbc>

\(\hat{x}(Y)=\mathrm{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{P}(Y|X=x)=\mathrm{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal{C}}Z_{x,Y},\)

<tbc>since as a function of \(x\in\{0,1\}^N\), it holds that \(\mathbb{P}(Y|X=x)\propto Z_{x,Y}\). Thus, we have that<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}\left(\hat{x}(Y)\neq X\right)\le\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{x^\prime,Y}\ge Z_{X,Y}\text{for some}x'\in\mathcal{C}\backslash\{X\}\right)\le(|\mathcal{C}|-1)\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{X^\prime,Y}\ge Z_{X,Y}\right).\)

<tbc>But note that, since \(X'\) is independent of _X_, \(Z_{X^\prime,Y}\) and _Z<sub>X,Y</sub>_ are exactly distributed as the partition functions of the null and planted variants of the Random Subsequence Model, respectively. Hence, if one shows that the planted partition function is greater than the null partition function with high probability, that gives a bound on the maximum-likelihood decoder’s probability of failure. This maximum likelihood decoding strategy, combined with the sub-optimal bound

\(\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{X^\prime,Y}\ge Z_{X,Y}\right)\le\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{X^\prime,Y}\ge 1\right),\)

is the heart of the argument of \[Gal61; Zig69; DG01\], which gave one of the early lower bounds on the capacity of the deletion channel.

## 1.1.2. _Longest common subsequence of two random strings._

A second source of motivation for the Random Subsequence Model comes from the longest common subsequence (LCS) problem. If _X_<sub>1</sub> and _X_<sub>2</sub> are independent uniformly random binary strings of respective lengths _N_<sub>1</sub> and _N_<sub>2</sub>, we let LCS(_X_<sub>1</sub>_,X_<sub>2</sub>) denote the length of their longest common subsequence. A classical open problem of more than fifty years is to determine the limit<tbc>

\(f(\gamma):=\mathrm{lim}_{N_1,N_2\rightarrow\infty N_2/N_1=\gamma}\frac{1}{N_1}\mathbb{E}\left[\text{LCS}(X_1,X_2)\right].\)

<tbc>The case \(\gamma=1\), proposed by \[CS75\], has been the subject of intensive study \[Dek79; Ste82; Ale94; DP95; Hei+24\]. Following \[Bou99\], one may instead study the partition function<tbc>

\(Z_{N_1,N_2,M}:=|\{\sigma^1\in\Sigma_{N_1,M},\sigma^2\in\Sigma_{N_2,M}:(X_1)_{\sigma^1}=(X_2)_{\sigma^2}\}|,\)

<tbc>which counts common length-_M_ subsequences of _X_<sub>1</sub> and _X_<sub>2</sub>. So in particular, _Z_<sub>_N_<sub>1</sub>_,N_<sub>2</sub>_,M_</sub>_\>_0 if and only if there exists a common subsequence between _X_<sub>1</sub> and _X_<sub>2</sub> of length _M_. Then one can compute the associated free energy<tbc>

\(g(\gamma,\alpha):=\mathrm{lim}_{N_1,N_2,M\rightarrow\infty N_2/N_1=\gamma,M/N_1=\alpha}\frac{1}{N_1}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}(1+Z_{N_1,N_2,M})\right].\)

<tbc>This free energy encodes the LCS constant, as it is easy to show that<tbc>

\(f(\gamma)=\mathrm{sup}\left\{\alpha:g(\gamma,\alpha)>0\right\}.\)

<tbc>The null variant of our Random Subsequence Model corresponds to the special case where \(\gamma=\alpha\). Indeed, in that case one has _M=N_<sub>2</sub>, and then the second ambient string is itself the candidate subsequence, so

\(Z_{N_1,N_2,M}=|\{\sigma\in\Sigma_{N_1,M}:(X_1)_\sigma=X_2\}|=Z_{X_1,X_2},\)

<tbc>which is exactly (1.1). Thus, the Random Subsequence Model may be viewed as a natural slice of the partition-function framework for the longest common subsequence problem. We therefore believe that a better understanding of the Random Subsequence Model is likely to be of interest for the longest common subsequence problem as well.

Lastly, we also note that longest common subsequences play a central role in deletion coding more broadly \[GHL22\]. For adversarial deletions, extremal bounds on pairwise LCS govern codebook feasibility, and even the analysis of random deletion codes is limited by the current lack of sharp estimates for the expected LCS of two random binary strings.

## 1.1.3. _Mean-field variants and directed polymers._

Our third and final connection is to _directed polymers_ in statistical physics. This connection is nontrivial, and will help us frame the discussion by using the experience of the directed polymers literature to identify which models can be expected to admit exact analytic solutions (see Section 1.2).

Given \((X,Y)\in\{0,1\}^N\times\{0,1\}^M\), \(n\le N\) and \(m\le M\), we use _X_<sub>1:_n_</sub>_,Y_<sub>1:_m_</sub> to denote the prefixes of _X,Y_ from index 1 to _n,m_, respectively. We also denote<tbc>

\(Z_{n,m}:=Z_{X_{1:n},Y_{1:m}},\)

<tbc>noting that _Z<sub>N,M</sub>=Z<sub>X,Y</sub>_. By partitioning<tbc>

\(S_{X_{1:n},Y_{1:m}}=(S_{X_{1:n},Y_{1:m}}\cap\{\sigma_m=n\})\sqcup(S_{X_{1:n},Y_{1:m}}\cap\{\sigma_m\neq n\}),\)

<tbc>we observe the recurrence relation

(1.4) \(Z_{n,m}=Z_{n-1,m}+\unknown\{X_n=Y_m\}\cdot Z_{n-1,m-1}.\)

Note that the above gives an efficient dynamic programming algorithm to compute _Z<sub>N,M</sub>_ exactly. It also leads to a natural generalization of our model. Rather than specifying two strings _X_ and _Y_, we can instead specify a matrix \(B\in\mathbb{R}_+^{N\times M}\) and _define_ the partition function _Z<sub>N,M</sub>_ via the recurrence relation

(1.5) \(Z_{n,m}=Z_{n-1,m}+B_{n,m}\cdot Z_{n-1,m-1},1\le n\le N,1\le m\le M,\)

with the initial condition \(Z_{0,m}=\delta_{0,m}\). This can be interpreted as a directed polymer model, and in the case that _B_ has entries in {0,1}, a directed percolation model, in a random environment determined by _B_. Indeed, consider a box in Z<sup>2</sup> with bottom-left endpoint at (0,0) and top-right endpoint at (_N,M_). Put an edge between any two horizontal neighbors (_n_-1_,m),(n,m_) with weight 1 and an edge between diagonal neighbors (_n_-1_,m_-1),(_n,m_) with weight _B<sub>n,m</sub>_. Then _Z<sub>N,M</sub>_ counts weighted paths from (0,0) to (_N,M_) that are monotonically increasing in the first coordinate.

This kind of model has received considerable attention in the directed polymers literature. An insight of those investigations is that only distributions of _B_ with special algebraic structure admit exact analytic solutions with existing techniques. The case where _B_ has i.i.d. Gamma-distributed entries falls in that category, and its exact analytic solution was found in the important work \[CSS15\]. We refer the reader to the next section for a discussion of how this relates to the Random Subsequence Model. As far as the authors are aware, the Random Subsequence Model itself, which corresponds to a natural "rank-one" random environment _B_, has not been explicitly studied in the directed polymers literature. Cases where the entries of _B_ are i.i.d. represent a natural _mean field_ version of the Random Subsequence Model, and the setting where _B_ has i.i.d. Unif{0,1} entries has been studied under the name "Bernoulli Matching Model" in connection to the longest common subsequence problem (see \[Bou99; MN05\]).

## 1.2. Our results.

Our first result gives strict bounds on the free energies of the null and planted variants of the Random Subsequence Model. For the rest of the paper, following the statistical physics terminology, we use the term _annealed_ free energy to refer to the quantities of the form

\(\frac{1}{N}log\mathbb{E}[Z],\)

<tbc>i.e., with the expectation _inside_ the log. This is in contrast to the default, _quenched_ free energy

\(\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}[logZ],\)

where the expectation is outside the log.

**Theorem 1.1** (Quenched-annealed gaps)**.** _Fix_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\)_. Let_ \(X,X'\in\{0,1\}^N\) _be independent uniform random strings and let_ \(Y\in\{0,1\}^M\) _be a uniform random length-M subsequence of X (with_ \(M=\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor\)_). Defining_<tbc>

\(f_\mathrm{null}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha):=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}log\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{X^\prime,Y}\right],\)

<tbc>_there exists a constant_ \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)>0\) _such that_

(1.6) \(\frac{1}{N}logZ_{X,Y}-\rightarrow^pf_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)>f_\mathrm{null}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha),\)

_where_ \(-\rightarrow^p\) _denotes convergence in probability. Moreover, if_ \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\)_, then there exists a constant_ \(f_\mathrm{null}(\alpha)>0\) _such that_

(1.7) \(\frac{1}{N}logZ_{X^\prime,Y}-\rightarrow^pf_\mathrm{null}(\alpha)\)

_and this constant satisfies_

(1.8) \(h(2\alpha)/2\le f_\mathrm{null}(\alpha)<f_\mathrm{null}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha).\)

The threshold \(\alpha=1/2\) is the natural boundary for the weak limit (1.7) to hold under the null model. Indeed, as discussed at the beginning of Section 2, it is easy to show that \(Z_{X^\prime,Y}=0\) with high probability for \(\alpha>1/2\) and that at the boundary \(\alpha=1/2\), there does not exist a weak limit of the form (1.7) for the null model. Additionally, the main quantitative result in Section 3 which separates the exponential behavior of \(Z_{X^\prime,Y}\) from the annealed free energy of the null model, namely (3.34), holds for all \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) (though with implicit constants depending on the choice of \(\alpha\)). Together with Theorem 1.1, these observations give strict exponential-scale bounds for the Random Subsequence Model throughout the entire dense regime \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). We record in Appendix B a combinatorial consequence of (1.8), showing in particular that there is no further transition in the relation between \(f_\mathrm{null}(\alpha)\) and \(f_\mathrm{null}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)\) within the range \(\alpha<1/2\).

We now connect Theorem 1.1 to channel coding over the binary deletion channel with uniform random codes; see [PIW24] for a more complete discussion of this viewpoint. For \(p\in[0,1]\), we let \(C_\mathrm{unif}(p)\in[0,1]\) denote the maximum rate achievable through the deletion channel with deletion probability _p_ using uniform random codes, i.e., the quantity that was introduced in (1.2).

**Corollary 1.2** (Positive rate for uniform codes; [PIW24, Conjecture 3])**.** _It holds for all deletion probabilities_ \(p\in[0,1)\) _that C_<sub>unif</sub>(_p)\>_0.

Corollary 1.2 confirms [PIW24, Conjecture 3] and resolves [PIW24, Question 1] by showing that uniformly random codes achieve a strictly positive rate even when \(p\ge 1/2\), i.e., in the regime where each bit is more likely to be deleted than retained. This is the first such positive-rate result for uniform codebooks in this regime, and it strengthens (in a qualitative sense) the earlier lower bounds of [Gal61; Zig69; DG01; DM06; RD13; HOS16], all of which were only able to address the _p\<_1/2 setting.

In fact, the proof of Theorem 1.1 yields a quantitative version of Corollary 1.2 in the likely deletion regime. Specifically, there exists \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) (the crude explicit bound of Theorem 3.13 gives _k_=362, which we expect to be far from sharp) such that as \(p\rightarrow 1\),<tbc>

\(C_\mathrm{unif}(p)=\Omega\big((1-p)^k\big).\)

<tbc>On the other hand, as \(p\rightarrow 1\), [DSV12] gives the upper bound

\(C_\mathrm{unif}(p)=O\left((1-p)^{4/3}log\frac{1}{1-p}\right).\)

These bounds together show that the uniform capacity decays polynomially but faster than linearly in 1-_p_ as \(p\rightarrow 1\). We note that \(f_\mathrm{null}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)\) trivially admits an exact analytic formula. Indeed, we have \(f_\mathrm{null}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\mathbb{E}[Z_{X^\prime,Y}]\)
\(=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\left(|\Sigma_{N,M}|2^{-M}\right)=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\left(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{M}2^{-M}\right)=h(\alpha)-\alpha\mathrm{log}2.\) The situation is significantly more involved for the annealed free energy of the planted model \(f_\mathrm{pl}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\mathbb{E}[Z_{X,Y}].\) However, our next result gives an exact analytic formula for this quantity as well. **Theorem 1.3** (Annealed free energy of the planted model)**.** _For every_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\)_, define_ \(\Delta(\alpha)=\sqrt{9\alpha^2-4\alpha+4};x_\alpha=\frac{\Delta(\alpha)-3\alpha}{2};y_\alpha=\frac{(3\alpha+2-\Delta(\alpha))^2}{2(\Delta(\alpha)-3\alpha)(2+\Delta(\alpha)-3\alpha)}.\) _Then_ \((x_\alpha,y_\alpha)\in(0,\infty)^2\) _and_ \(f_\mathrm{pl}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)=-h(\alpha)-\alpha\mathrm{log}2-\mathrm{log}x_\alpha-\alpha\mathrm{log}y_\alpha.\) Note that, by Jensen’s inequality, \(f_\mathrm{pl}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)\) is an upper bound on \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\). Combining this with (1.3) yields an upper bound on the uniform capacity of the deletion channel for all deletion probabilities. We note that this is one of the very few known analytic bounds for the deletion channel [DG01; Che19], and is numerically far closer than any other upper bounds of which we are aware, albeit bounding the uniform capacity rather than the full capacity. We view this as further evidence that the uniform capacity is a fruitful stepping stone towards better understanding the full capacity problem. Finally, we note that [PIW24] previously gave an efficient _algorithm_ to compute the annealed free energy in the planted model to any desired precision. Our result significantly improves on theirs by being exact and analytic. We conclude this section by returning to the connection with directed polymers. As we mentioned in Section 1.1, the Random Subsequence Model can be understood as a directed polymer model in a random "rank-one" environment. In the directed polymer literature, only models with special algebraic structure have been found to admit exact solutions. Since this kind of structure does not seem to be present in the Random Subsequence Model, the experience of the directed polymer literature suggests that it may be intractable to obtain exact analytic formulas for _f_pl or _f_null with existing mathematical techniques, and results of the kind proved in Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 may be the best we can hope for. However, we think that a promising direction is to study variants of the Random Subsequence Model which do admit such exact solutions. There is a long tradition of doing this in the literature on spin glasses. For example, the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, which led to tremendous progress, was first proposed as a simplified, mean-field version of the earlier Edwards-Anderson model [EA75; SK75]. In our case, the natural solvable analogue is the Strict-Weak Polymer Model, introduced and solved in [CSS15]. After a trivial mapping, this corresponds to exactly the same recurrence as (1.5), but where we take _B_ to have i.i.d. Gamma(_a,b_) entries. The exact solution in this case is (see [CSS15, Theorem 1.3]) (1.9) \(\mathrm{lim}_{N,M\rightarrow\infty M/N=\alpha}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}Z_{N,M}\right]=\mathrm{inf}_{\lambda>0}\left\{-(1-\alpha)\Psi(\lambda)+\Psi(a+\lambda)+\alpha\mathrm{log}b\right\},\) where \(\Psi\) is the digamma function \(\Psi(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\mathrm{log}\Gamma(x)=\frac{\Gamma'(x)}{\Gamma(x)}.\)

<tbc>We can choose _a_ and _b_ so as to agree with the null variant of the Random Subsequence Model as much as possible by insisting that the entries of _B_ have the same mean and variance as they would in the Random Subsequence Model. This amounts to choosing _a_=1_,b_=1/2, which corresponds to the entries of _B_ being i.i.d. Exponential(2). In Figure 2, we plot the exact solution (1.9) alongside the numerical solution of (1.4) for the null Random Subsequence Model. The fact that the two curves are very close suggests that the Strict-Weak Polymer Model may be fruitful to study to gain insight on the Random Subsequence Model. We pose some open problems in this direction in Section 5.

## 1.3. Outline of the proofs.

We now sketch the proofs of the main results, focusing on the key mechanisms that drive the analysis and postponing the technical details to the body of the paper.

### 1.3.1. _Proof overview of Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2._

The convergence statements in (1.6) and (1.7) are essentially obtained in Section 2 by invoking the superadditive ergodic theorem on the log-partition function of the model. In the planted model, \(logZ_{X,\text{BDC}_{1-\alpha}(X)}\) is genuinely superadditive, and a coupling between \(\text{BDC}_{1-\alpha}(X)\) and a uniform length-_M_ subsequence transfers the weak limit to the fixed-length planted model. Rare occurrences can break this superadditivity in the null model, so we instead prove the weak law by directly exploiting the self-replicating structure of the subsequence count. We also obtain the first lower bound of (1.8) by encoding embeddings of \(S_{X^\prime,Y}\) via _skip vectors_, which record at each step how many occurrences of the current target bit are passed over a greedy embedding procedure. Realizing a vector with _s_ total skips is equivalent to requiring that a sum of _M+s_ i.i.d. Geom(1/2) random variables be at most _N_.

\(\mathcal{G}(x)\subseteq\{0,1\}^M\)

of strings that are "well-aligned" to _x_ so that we obtain the following distinguishing property.

\(\bullet\) For (_X,Y_) drawn from the planted model, \(Y\in\mathcal{G}(X)\) with probability \(1-e^{-\Omega(N)}\).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) For \((X',Y)\) drawn from the null model, \(Y\notin\mathcal{G}(X')\) with probability \(1-e^{-\Omega(N)}\).

The strict inequality of (1.8) is then obtained by showing that for typical _x_, only an exponentially small fraction of its length-_M_ subsequences belong to G(_x_). The strict inequality of (1.6) essentially comes from combining this null estimate with the size-bias relation between the null and planted laws.

To define G(_x_), we partition _x_ into _B=B(N_):=_N/b_ contiguous blocks _x_<sup>(1)</sup>_,...,x_<sup>(_B_)</sup> of length _b_, where _b_ is large but fixed. If _Y_ is a planted subsequence of _x_, then the embedding induces a decomposition<tbc>

\(Y=\big(Y^{(1)},\dots,Y^{(B)}\big),\)

For a typical block of _x_, the sign of the block sum in _Y_ <sup>(_i_)</sup> is more likely than not to agree with that of _x_<sup>(_i_)</sup>, and the strength of this bias is captured by the random-walk displacement \(\Delta(Y^{(i)})\). Here _Y_ is independent of \(X'\), and we must rule out the possibility that an adversary can produce an induced near-equipartition of _Y_ so as to mimic the macroscopic block structure of \(X'\). This is difficult because it can be shown that

(1) many natural block statistics can be driven above 1/2 by a favorable induced near-equipartition, so one needs a score that is robust under adversarial choices;<tbc>

(2) there are exponentially many induced near-equipartitions of _Y_ , and this family is large enough that standard metric entropy arguments over the collection of all such induced near-equipartitions do not provide appropriate guarantees.

The notions of alignment introduced above are so that we may overcome the first obstacle. Our main device for overcoming the second obstacle is the _standardization algorithm_. This algorithm defines a map<tbc>

\(\varphi_Y:\mathcal{N}\mathcal{E}_\text{ind}(Y)\rightarrow\mathcal{N}\mathcal{E}_\text{std}(Y),\)

<tbc>sending induced near-equipartitions of _Y_ to a much smaller class of _standardized near-equipartitions_ in which almost all block lengths are some fixed length. \(T_\text{std}(X',Y)<\frac{1+\beta^\star(\alpha)}{2}\)

with overwhelming probability. Hence, \(Y\notin\mathcal{G}(X')\).

(1.10) \(\mathbb{P}\left(Z_{X^\prime,Y}<e^{N\left(f_\text{null}^\text{ann}(\alpha)-\Omega(1)\right)}\right)\ge 1-e^{-\Omega(N)}.\)

This implies that \(f_\text{null}(\alpha)<f_\text{null}^\text{ann}(\alpha)\). ## 1.3.2. _Proof overview of Theorem 1.3._

The starting point of the proof is to rewrite the planted annealed partition function in a way that exposes the geometry of _pairs_ of embeddings rather than individual embeddings. Indeed, a simple argument leads to the formula<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{X,Y}\right]=\frac{1}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{M}2^M}\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma} 2^{\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle},\)

<tbc>where \(\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle\) denotes the _overlap_

\(\sum_{j=1}^M\unknown\{\sigma(j)=\tau(j)\}.\)

Hence, the goal of the rest of the proof is to understand the moment generating function of the overlap of a random pair of configurations. The key structural property used to understand this is a certain Markov

<tbc>property for the distribution of \((\sigma,\tau)\sim\Sigma^2\) : if we select indices \(i\in[N]\) and \(j\in[M]\) and condition on the event that \(\sigma(j)=\tau(j)=i\), then the pairs<tbc>

\((\sigma|_{[j-1]},\tau|_{[j-1]}),(\sigma|_{[M]\backslash[j]},\tau|_{[M]\backslash[j]})\)

<tbc>become conditionally independent and, after a trivial relabeling, uniform in \(\Sigma_{i-1,j-1}^2,\Sigma_{N-i,M-j}^2\), respectively. This leads to a recursive structure for the moment generating function which underlies the proof of Lemma 4.1. This lemma proves the formula<tbc>

(1.11) \(\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma} 2^{\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle}=\sum_{\ell=0}^M\sum_{1\le j_1<\cdots<j_\ell\le M}\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_\ell\le N}\prod_{k=1}^{\ell+1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{i_k-i_{k-1}-1}{j_k-j_{k-1}-1}^2\)

<tbc>where we define _i_<sub>0</sub>=_j_<sub>0</sub>=0 and \(i_{\ell+1}=N+1,j_{\ell+1}=M+1\). The benefit of this formula is that the expression inside the summand depends on the tuples \((j_1,\dots,j_\ell)\) and \((i_1,\dots,i_\ell)\) only through the empirical measure<tbc>

\(\mu=\frac{1}{\ell+1}\sum_{k=1}^{\ell+1}\delta_{(i_k-i_{k-1},j_k-j_{k-1})}\)

<tbc>supported on \(\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2\). This is finite-dimensional, so as \(N,M\rightarrow\infty\), (1.11) turns into a constrained variational problem in the space of probability measures in \(\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2\). Indeed, the limit of the log of (1.11) normalized by _N_ is shown to be<tbc>

\(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=sup_{\rho\in(0,1)}\alpha\rho\Phi(\rho),\)

<tbc>where for each fixed \(\rho\), the inner quantity \(\Phi(\rho)\) is the supremum of<tbc>

\(H(\nu)+\mathbb{E}_\nu[logw(a,b)],\)

<tbc>where _H_ is the Shannon entropy and \(w(a,b)=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{a-1}{b-1}^2\), over probability measures \(\nu\) supported in \(\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2\) satisfying the mean constraints

\(\mathbb{E}_{(a,b)\sim\nu}[a]=\frac{1}{\alpha\rho},\mathbb{E}_{(a,b)\sim\nu}[b]=\frac{1}{\rho}.\)

Conceptually, this is the heart of the proof: all of the combinatorics has now been absorbed into a finite- dimensional order parameter, namely the law solving the variational problem \(\Phi(\rho)\).

The second half of the argument is to solve this variational problem explicitly. For fixed \(\rho\), one introduces Lagrange multipliers for the normalization and moment constraints. This shows that the maximizing measure must lie in an exponential family:<tbc>

\(\nu^*(a,b)\propto w(a,b)x^ay^b\)

<tbc>for suitable parameters _x,y\>_0. Thus the optimization is encoded by a two-variable partition function

\(Z(x,y)=\sum_{a\ge 1}\sum_{1\le b\le a}w(a,b)x^ay^b.\)

The value of the variational problem can then be expressed in terms of log_Z(x,y_) together with the moment constraints. The next step is therefore analytic rather than probabilistic: one computes _Z(x,y_) in closed form. This is done by rewriting the sum using Vandermonde’s identity and then evaluating the resulting generating function explicitly.

Once the inner variational problem over \(\nu\) has been solved, one returns to the outer optimization in \(\rho\). Here the key observation is that at an interior optimizer, the envelope theorem implies that the derivative of the outer objective is proportional to log_Z(x,y_). Hence optimality forces the normalization condition

\(Z(x,y)=1.\)

This is what collapses the remaining optimisation to a purely algebraic system. Combining the equation _Z(x,y_)=1 with the stationarity relation coming from the moment constraints yields two equations in the

<tbc>two unknowns _x_ and _y_. Solving this system produces the explicit formulas for \(x_\alpha\) and \(y_\alpha\), and substituting them back gives

\(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=-\mathrm{log}x_\alpha-\alpha\mathrm{log}y_\alpha,\)

which concludes the proof.

Unless otherwise stated, all asymptotics are taken as \(N,M\rightarrow\infty\) with \(\alpha=M/N\) fixed, and we omit floor and ceiling symbols when doing so does not affect asymptotic behavior. Because many of our estimates are meaningful only up to subexponential factors, we introduce the shorthand

\(f(N)\approx g(N)\Longleftrightarrow\frac{f(N)}{g(N)}=e^{o(N)}\text{and}\frac{g(N)}{f(N)}=e^{o(N)}.\)

It is immediate that ≈ defines an equivalence relation on functions from N to R<sub>_\>_0</sub>. ### 1.5. Organization.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we prove the lower bound of (1.8) and establish the weak limits of (1.6) and (1.7). Proving the strict inequalities of (1.6) and (1.8) constitutes the main technical challenge of the proof of Theorem 1.1. We carry this out in Section 3 and then establish Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2. In Section 4, we derive the exact annealed free energy formula of Theorem 1.3. We conclude in Section 5 with some open problems and suggestions for future research.

## 2. Weak Limits for the Null and Planted Models

We initiate the proof of Theorem 1.1 by establishing the existence of weak limits \(f_\mathrm{null}(\alpha)>0\) (for values \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\) of the density parameter) and \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)>0\) for which (1.6) and (1.7) hold.

### 2.1. Null model.

Throughout Section 2.1, we fix \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\). We begin by observing that the existence of the weak limit \(f_\mathrm{null}(\alpha)\) is enough to prove the first inequality of (1.8). Towards this end, we first observe that there is a natural greedy algorithm [DG01; Mit09] for attempting to embed _Y_ into \(X'\). Writing \(\tau(i)\) for the position selected at step _i_ and setting \(\tau(0):=0\), we define \(\tau(i)\) recursively as the least index \(t>\tau(i-1)\) such that \(X'_t=Y_i\) whenever such an index exists. If no such index exists at some step, we say that the greedy embedding algorithm fails. Then<tbc>

\(Z_{X^\prime,Y}=0\Longleftrightarrow\text{the greedy embedding algorithm fails,}\)

<tbc>since any \(\sigma\in S_{X^\prime,Y}\) must satisfy \(\tau(i)\le\sigma(i)\) at every step for which the greedy algorithm is defined. Equivalently, the event that \(Z_{X^\prime,Y}=0\) is exactly the event that

\(\sum_{i=1}^MG_i>N,\)

where _G_<sub>1</sub>_,...,G<sub>M</sub>_ are i.i.d. Geom(1/2) random variables. Here, _G<sub>i</sub>_ corresponds to the number of bits of \(X'\) that must be examined after \(\tau(i-1)\) in order to locate \(\tau(i)\). It easily follows from this latter representation that \(Z_{X^\prime,Y}=0\) with high probability for \(\alpha>1/2\), and that at \(\alpha=1/2\), the event \(Z_{X^\prime,Y}=0\) has probability tending to 1/2. This explains why the weak limit (1.7) is stated only for \(\alpha\in(0,1/2)\).

We now fix \(\sigma\in S_{X^\prime,Y}\), which corresponds to the following _skip vector_ \(v\in\mathbb{N}^M\). For each \(i\in[M]\), we let _v<sub>i</sub>_ denote the number of instances of _Y<sub>i</sub>_ strictly after the earliest instance of _Y<sub>i</sub>_ following \(X'_{\sigma(i-1)}\) (for _i_=1, this is the earliest instance of _Y_<sub>1</sub> in \(X'\)) up to and including \(X'_{\sigma(i)}\). We think of _v<sub>i</sub>_ as the number of

<tbc>_skips_ that the _i_th bit of _Y_ plays over the greedy algorithm when constructing \(\sigma\). This mapping from \(S_{X^\prime,Y}\) to skip vectors \(v\in\mathbb{N}^M\) is evidently injective. Furthermore, for each \(s\in\mathbb{N}\), we define<tbc>

\(\mathcal{V}_s:=\left\{v\in\mathbb{N}^M:\sum_{i=1}^Mv_i=s\right\}.\)

<tbc>It similarly follows that for any \(v\in\mathcal{V}_s\), the event that _v_ is a skip vector corresponding to a configuration in \(S_{X^\prime,Y}\) is the event that the sum of _M+s_ i.i.d. Geom(1/2) random variables is at most _N_. Here, each Geom(1/2) random variable corresponds to the number of bits of \(X'\) necessary to advance the candidate embedding with skip vector _v_ by one step. We conclude that

\(Z_{X^\prime,Y}=\sum_{s=0}^{(1/\alpha-1)M}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_s}\unknown\left\{v\text{corresponds to an elmt. of}S_{X^\prime,Y}\right\}\ge\sum_{s=0}^{\left(\frac{1}{2\alpha}-1\right)M}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_s}\unknown\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{M+s}\text{Geom}(1/2)\le N\right\}\ge e^{-o_p(N)}\sum_{s=0}^{\left(\frac{1}{2\alpha}-1\right)M}\left|\mathcal{V}_s\right|\approx e^{-o_p(N)}\big|\mathcal{V}_{\left(\frac{1}{2\alpha}-1\right)M}\approx e^{-o_p(N)}exp\left(M\cdot\frac{h(2\alpha)}{2\alpha}\right)=e^{-o_p(N)}exp\left(N\cdot\frac{h(2\alpha)}{2}\right),\text{(2.1)}\)

where the latter inequality of (2.1) follows from Cramér’s theorem applied to the Geom(1/2) law and Markov’s inequality to control the number of "bad summands." The lower bound of (1.8) follows.

It remains to prove (1.7). Our strategy is guided by the observation that \(Z_{X^\prime,Y}\) exhibits an approximate superadditivity due to its self-replicating structure. For large integers _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub>, the inequality

(2.2) \(logZ_{X_{1:N_1+N_2}^\prime Y_{1:M_1+M_2}}\ge logZ_{X_{1:N_1}^\prime,Y_{1:M_1}}+logZ_{X_{N_1+1:N_1+N_2}^\prime,Y_{M_1+1:M_1+M_2}},\)

\(\mathcal{NE}_\mathrm{std}(y):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c }

With the machinery of Section 3.1 in place, we are now ready to introduce the regular alignment property, which is the key notion of structural alignment between binary strings which we exploit to prove the upper bound of Theorem 1.1. Thus, for fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), it holds that (3.40) \(0<^\text{(1.6)}f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)-f_\mathrm{null}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)=f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)-\left(h(\alpha)-\alpha log2\right)=^\text{(3.39)}C_\mathrm{unif}(1-\alpha).\) We conclude that \(d_\mathrm{unif}^*=1\), as desired. □

### 3.5.2. _Explicit capacity lower bound._ We now revisit the proof of Theorem 1.1, keeping track of constants in order to obtain an explicit strictly positive lower bound on _C_unif(_p_). Towards this end, for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), we define the quantity \(\kappa(\alpha):=\left\lceil\frac{1920^{96}}{\alpha^{24}\beta(\alpha)^{96}(1-\alpha)^{12}}\right\rceil.\) We stress that we do not attempt to optimize the resulting bound; our objective is simply to extract a fully explicit positive capacity lower bound for uniform random codebooks in the likely deletion regime. **Theorem 3.13** (Explicit capacity lower bound)**.** _For_ \(p\in(0,1)\)_, we have that_ \(C_\mathrm{unif}(p)\ge\frac{\left(\beta(1-p)\right)^3}{51200\cdot\left(\kappa(1-p)\right)^5}>0.\) Since the proof of Theorem 3.13 mainly consists of verifying a collection of routine inequalities and parameter constraints, we defer it to Appendix D. ## 4. Annealed Free Energy Under the Planted Model In this section, we derive an exact formula for the _annealed free energy_ of the planted model, \(f_\mathrm{pl}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{X,Y}\right],\) which by Jensen gives an upper bound on \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\). We note that \[PIW24\] gave an efficient algorithm to approximate \(f_\mathrm{pl}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha)\) to any desired precision. Here we improve on their result by proving Theorem 1.3 and giving an exact asymptotic formula. It will be convenient for us to identify sets \(S\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{[N]}{M}\) with functions \(\sigma\in\Sigma=\Sigma_{N,M}\) such that \(\mathrm{Im}(\sigma)=S\). Moreover, for \(\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma\), we use the notations \(I(\sigma,\tau)=\{j\in[M]:\sigma_j=\tau_j\};\)
\(\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^M\unknown\{\sigma_j=\tau_j\}=|I(\sigma,\tau)|.\) Given a string \(X\in\{0,1\}^N\), we use the notation \(X_\sigma:=X|_{\mathrm{Im}(\sigma)}.\) Note that we have \(\mathbb{E}\left[Z_{X,Y}\right]=\frac{1}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{M}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{M}}\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma}\mathbb{P}\left(X_\sigma=X_\tau\right)=\frac{1}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{M}}\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma} 2^{-\left(M-\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle\right)}=\frac{1}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{M}2^M}\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma} 2^{\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle}.\) Hence, to prove Theorem 1.3, it suffices to show that, letting \(\overline{Z}=\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma} 2^{\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle},\) we have (4.1) \(\mathrm{lim}_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\overline{Z}=-\mathrm{log}x_\alpha-\alpha\mathrm{log}y_\alpha.\) The remainder of Section 4 proves (4.1) and hence Theorem 1.3. We begin from the elementary identity \(2^{\langle\sigma,\tau\rangle}=\sum_{J\subseteq I(\sigma,\tau)}1=\sum_{\ell=0}^M\sum_{J\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{[M]}{\ell}}\unknown\{J\subseteq I(\sigma,\tau)\}.\)

<tbc>Summing over \(\sigma,\tau\) yields

(4.2) \(\overline{Z}=\sum_{\ell=0}^M\sum_{J\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{[M]}{\ell}}\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\Sigma}\unknown\{J\subseteq I(\sigma,\tau)\}.\)

Fix \(\ell\) and \(J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_\ell\}\). If \(J\subseteq I(\sigma,\tau)\) then \(\sigma_{j_r}=\tau_{j_r}\) for each _r_, and these common values form an increasing \(\ell\)-tuple \(K=\{i_1<\cdots<i_\ell\}\subseteq[N]\). Thus<tbc>

\(\unknown\{J\subseteq I(\sigma,\tau)\}=\sum_{K\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{[N]}{\ell}}\unknown\{\sigma_{j_r}=\tau_{j_r}=i_r\text{for all}r\in[\ell]\}.\)

<tbc>Insert this in (4.2) and exchange sums to obtain

(4.3) \(\overline{Z}=\sum_{\ell=0}^M\sum_{1\le j_1<\cdots<j_\ell\le M}\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_\ell\le N}\big|\{\sigma\in\Sigma:\sigma_{j_r}=i_r\text{for all}r\in[\ell]\}\big|^2,\)

where the square comes from the independence of \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) given the constraints.

## 4.1. Counting constrained increasing maps.

Fix \(j_1<\cdots<j_\ell\) and \(i_1<\cdots<i_\ell\). Set the convenient boundary values<tbc>

\(i_0:=0,j_0:=0,i_{\ell+1}:=N+1,j_{\ell+1}:=M+1.\)

<tbc>For each \(k\in[\ell+1]\), consider the interval of _positions_ {_j_<sub>_k_-1</sub>+1_,...,j<sub>k</sub>_-1} of size _j<sub>k</sub>-j_<sub>_k_-1</sub>-1, whose values must lie strictly between _i_<sub>_k_-1</sub> and _i<sub>k</sub>_. There are exactly _i<sub>k</sub>-i_<sub>_k_-1</sub>-1 available integers in {_i_<sub>_k_-1</sub>+1_,...,i<sub>k</sub>_-1}, and choosing which of those occupy the _j<sub>k</sub>-j_<sub>_k_-1</sub>-1 slots uniquely determines \(\sigma\) on that interval by monotonicity. Therefore,

\(\big|\{\sigma\in\Sigma_{N,M}:\sigma_{j_r}=i_r\text{for all}r\in[\ell]\}\big|=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell+1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{i_k-i_{k-1}-1}{j_k-j_{k-1}-1}.\)

Plugging into (4.3) gives the following explicit form.

**Lemma 4.1** (Gap product formula)**.** _For all_ \(1\le M\le N\),

\(\overline{Z}=\sum_{\ell=0}^M\sum_{1\le j_1<\cdots<j_\ell\le M}\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_\ell\le N}\prod_{k=1}^{\ell+1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{i_k-i_{k-1}-1}{j_k-j_{k-1}-1}^2,\)

_with the boundary convention i_<sub>0</sub>=_j_<sub>0</sub>=0 _and_ \(i_{\ell+1}=N+1\), \(j_{\ell+1}=M+1\).

## 4.2. From gaps to compositions.

For each \(k\in[\ell+1]\) define the positive integers<tbc>

\(a_k:=i_k-i_{k-1}\in\mathbb{N}_{>0},b_k:=j_k-j_{k-1}\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}.\)

<tbc>Then \(\sum_{k=1}^{\ell+1}a_k=N+1\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^{\ell+1}b_k=M+1\), and

\(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{i_k-i_{k-1}-1}{j_k-j_{k-1}-1}=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{a_k-1}{b_k-1}.\)

Conversely, any \((a_1,b_1),\dots,(a_{\ell+1},b_{\ell+1})\in(\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2)^{\ell+1}\) with those sum constraints uniquely determines \((i_1,\dots,i_\ell)\) and \((j_1,\dots,j_\ell)\) by partial summation. Thus, Lemma 4.1 can be rewritten as a sum over _block compositions_. We let

\(w(a,b):=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{a-1}{b-1}^2\text{for}a\ge 1,1\le b\le a,w(a,b):=0\text{otherwise},\)

<tbc>and for each \(\ell\ge 0\) we define<tbc>

\(\mathcal{S}_\ell(N,M):=\left\{(a_1,b_1),\dots,(a_{\ell+1},b_{\ell+1})\in(\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2)^{\ell+1}:\sum_{k=1}^{\ell+1}a_k=N+1,\sum_{k=1}^{\ell+1}b_k=M+1\right\}.\)

<tbc>Then writing \(L=\ell+1\), we have

(4.4) \(\overline{Z}=\sum_{L=1}^{M+1}\sum_{(X_1,\dots,X_L)\in\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(N,M)}\prod_{k=1}^Lw(X_k).\)

For a block tuple (_X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>L</sub>_) define its empirical measure<tbc>

\(\mu=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k=1}^L\delta_{X_k}.\)

<tbc>Let M_<sub>L</sub>_ denote the set of all empirical measures of the form above (i.e., _L_ atoms of weight 1_/L_, allowing repetitions). For \(\mu\in\mathcal{M}_L\), let \(\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)\) be the set of (ordered) tuples with empirical measure \(\mu\). Then we can rewrite

(4.5) \(\overline{Z}=\sum_{L=1}^{M+1}\sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{M}_L:\mathbb{E}_\mu[a]=\frac{N+1}{L},\mathbb{E}_\mu[b]=\frac{M+1}{L}}|\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)|exp\big(L\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw(a,b)]\big).\)

(The mean constraints are forced because \(\sum_kX_k=(N+1,M+1)\).)

## 4.3. Exponential scale of the entropy term.

Write<tbc>

\(n_{a,b}=n_{a,b}(\mu):=L\mu(a,b)\in\{0,1,\dots,L\}\)

<tbc>for the multiplicity of the value (_a,b_) under \(\mu\). Then the number of tuples with empirical measure \(\mu\) is the multinomial coefficient

(4.6) \(|\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)|=\frac{L!}{\prod_{(a,b)}n_{a,b}!}.\)

Recall the Shannon entropy

\(H(\mu):=-\sum_{a,b}\mu(a,b)log\mu(a,b),0log0:=0.\)

## 4.4. Entropy approximation and reduction to a variational problem.

Define the truncated-to-\(L\le M\) sum

(4.7) \(\overline{Z^{\le M}}:=\sum_{L=1}^M\sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{M}_L:\mathbb{E}_\mu[a]=\frac{N+1}{L},\mathbb{E}_\mu[b]=\frac{M+1}{L}}|\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)|exp\big(L\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw(a,b)]\big),\)

as well as the entropy-replaced sum

(4.8) \(\widetilde{Z}^{\le M}:=\sum_{L=1}^M\sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{M}_L:\mathbb{E}_\mu[a]=\frac{N+1}{L},\mathbb{E}_\mu[b]=\frac{M+1}{L}}exp\big(LH(\mu)+L\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw(a,b)]\big).\)

## 4.4.1. _Uniform Stirling decomposition._

**Lemma 4.2** (Uniform Stirling decomposition)**.** _Let_ \(L\ge 1\) _and_ \(\mu\in\mathcal{M}_L\) _with multiplicities_ \(n_{a,b}:=L\mu(a,b)\)_. Let_ \(D:=\{(a,b):n_{a,b}\ge 1\}\) _and s_:=|_D|. Then_

(4.9) \(log|\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)|=LH(\mu)+\frac{1}{2}log(2\pi L)-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(a,b)\in D}log(2\pi n_{a,b})+\rho_L(\mu),\)

_where the remainder satisfies the explicit bounds_

(4.10) \(-\sum_{(a,b)\in D}\frac{1}{12n_{a,b}}\le\rho_L(\mu)\le\frac{1}{12L}.\)

_Proof._ Apply the explicit Stirling bounds (valid for all integers \(k\ge 1\)),

\(\sqrt{2\pi k}\big(\frac{k}{e}\big)^k\le k!\le\sqrt{2\pi k}\big(\frac{k}{e}\big)^ke^\frac{1}{12k},\)

to \(log|\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)|=logL!-\sum_{(a,b)\in D}log(n_{a,b}!)\), and use \(LlogL-\sum_{a,b}n_{a,b}logn_{a,b}=LH(\mu)\). □

## 4.4.2. _Support bound and subexponential number of types._

For each _M_, we define the alphabet \(\mathcal{A}_M:=\big\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2:1\le b\le a\le N+1\big\}\), with<tbc>

\(K_M:=|\mathcal{A}_M|=\sum_{a=1}^{N+1}a=\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}.\)

<tbc>Let I_<sub>M</sub>_ denote the set of pairs \((L,\mu)\) that appear in (4.7), i.e.,<tbc>

\(\mathcal{I}_M:=\big\{(L,\mu):L\in\{1,\dots,M\},\mu\in\mathcal{M}_L,supp(\mu)\subseteq\mathcal{A}_M,\mathbb{E}_\mu[a]=\frac{N+1}{L},\mathbb{E}_\mu[b]=\frac{M+1}{L}\big\}.\)

<tbc>**Lemma 4.3** (Support bound)**.** _Let_ \((L,\mu)\in\mathcal{I}_M\)_, and write_ \(D:=supp(\mu)\)_. Then_<tbc>

(4.11) \(|D|\le\frac{1}{2}\big(\sqrt{3\sqrt{3(N+1)}}+2\big)^2.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Each distinct symbol (_a,b_) in _D_ appears at least once, hence

(4.12) \(\sum_{(a,b)\in supp(\mu)}a\le\sum_{k=1}^La_k=N+1.\)

For each \(a\ge 1\) there are exactly _a_ choices of \(b\in\{1,\dots,a\}\), and each such candidate pair (_a,b_) has "cost" _a_. We respectively denote the number of pairs with cost \(\le t\) and the total cost of all of them via<tbc>

\(N(t):=\sum_{a=1}^ta=\frac{t(t+1)}{2};C(t):=\sum_{a=1}^ta^2=\frac{t(t+1)(2t+1)}{6}.\)

<tbc>If _s_=|_D_|, let _t_ be the smallest integer with \(N(t)\ge s\), so that _N(t_-1)_\<s_. Then any set of _s_ pairs has total cost at least _C(t_-1). Hence

\(C(t-1)\le\sum_{(a,b)\in supp(\mu)}a\le^{(4.12)}N+1.\)

Using \(C(u)\ge u^3/3\) for \(u\ge 1\) gives \((t-1)^3/3\le N+1\), so \(t\le\sqrt{3\sqrt{3(N+1)}}+1\). Finally,

\(s\le N(t)=\frac{t(t+1)}{2}\le\frac{(t+1)^2}{2}\le\frac{1}{2}\big(\sqrt{3\sqrt{3(N+1)}}+2\big)^2,\)

producing the desired bound. □

<tbc>**Lemma 4.4** (Subexponential number of relevant types)**.** _We have_ \(lim_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}log|\mathcal{I}_M|=0\).

_Proof._ By Lemma 4.3, any feasible \(\mu\in\mathcal{M}_L\) has \(|supp(\mu)|\le s_M\) where _s<sub>M</sub>_ is the RHS of (4.11). For each \(s\le s_M\), the number of choices of a support set \(D\subseteq\mathcal{A}_M\) of size _s_ is \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{K_M}{s}\), and given _D_, the number of positive multiplicity vectors \((n_x)_{x\in D}\) with \(\sum_{x\in D}n_x=L\) is \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{L-1}{s-1}\). Hence the number of possible \(\mu\) satisfies<tbc>

\(|\mathcal{I}_M|\le\sum_{L=1}^M\sum_{s=1}^{\lfloor s_M\rfloor}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{K_M}{s}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{L-1}{s-1}.\)

<tbc>Using \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{K}{s}\le(eK/s)^s\) and the subadditivity of log yields

\(log|\mathcal{I}_M|\le s_M\cdot O(logM),\)

and since _s<sub>M</sub>=O(M_<sup>2/3</sup>) while \(N=M/\alpha\), we get \((1/N)log|\mathcal{I}_M|\rightarrow 0\). □

## 4.4.3. _Entropy replacement and sum-to-sup._

**Proposition 4.5** (Entropy replacement at scale _N_)**.** _Fix_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\)_. There exists an explicit deterministic_ \(\delta_M=\delta_M(\alpha)\) _with_ \(\delta_M/N\rightarrow 0\) _such that_<tbc>

(4.13) \(e^{-\delta_M}\widetilde{Z}^{\le M}\le\overline{Z^{\le M}}\le e^{\delta_M}\widetilde{Z}^{\le M}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Fix an admissible summand \((L,\mu)\) in (4.7) and write \(D=\{n_{a,b}\ge 1\}\), _s_=|_D_|. By Lemma 4.2,<tbc>

\(log|\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)|=LH(\mu)+\Delta_L(\mu)\)

<tbc>with \(\Delta_L(\mu)\) given by (4.9). Since \(1\le n_{a,b}\le L\le M\) on _D_, (4.10) implies<tbc>

\(|\Delta_L(\mu)|\le\frac{s+1}{2}log(2\pi M)+\frac{s}{12}+\frac{1}{12}.\)

<tbc>By Lemma 4.3, \(s\le s_M:=\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3(N+1)}+2)^2\) for every feasible \(\mu\), so \(|\Delta_L(\mu)|\le\delta_M\) with<tbc>

\(\delta_M:=\frac{s_M+1}{2}log(2\pi M)+\frac{s_M}{12}+\frac{1}{12},\frac{\delta_M}{N}\rightarrow 0.\)

<tbc>Thus, it holds uniformly over all admissible \((L,\mu)\) that

\(e^{-\delta_M}e^{LH(\mu)}\le|\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(\mu)|\le e^{\delta_M}e^{LH(\mu)}.\)

Multiplying by \(e^{L\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw]}\) and summing gives (4.13). □

**Proposition 4.6** (Sum to supremum)**.** _We have_

(4.14) \(\frac{1}{N}log\overline{Z^{\le M}}=sup_{(L,\mu)\in\mathcal{I}_M}\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\mu)+\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw(a,b)]\big)+o(1).\)

_Proof._ Let \(\widetilde{T}_M(L,\mu):=exp(LH(\mu)+L\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw])\). Since all summands are nonnegative,<tbc>

\(sup_{(L,\mu)\in\mathcal{I}_M}\widetilde{T}_M(L,\mu)\le\widetilde{Z}^{\le M}\le|\mathcal{I}_M|\cdot sup_{(L,\mu)\in\mathcal{I}_M}\widetilde{T}_M(L,\mu).\)

<tbc>Taking logs, dividing by _N_, and using Lemma 4.4 yields

\(\frac{1}{N}log\widetilde{Z}^{\le M}=sup_{(L,\mu)\in\mathcal{I}_M}\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\mu)+\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw]\big)+o(1).\)

Combine with Proposition 4.5 and \(\delta_M/N\rightarrow 0\) to replace \(\widetilde{Z}^{\le M}\) by \(\overline{Z^{\le M}}\). □

## 4.5. The limiting variational formula. For \(\rho\in(0,1)\) define \(\Phi(\rho):=sup\big\{H(\nu)+\mathbb{E}_\nu[logw(a,b)]:\text{supp}(\nu)\subseteq\{(a,b):1\le b\le a\},\) (4.15) \(|\text{supp}(\nu)|<\infty,\mathbb{E}_\nu[a]=\frac{1}{\alpha\rho},\mathbb{E}_\nu[b]=\frac{1}{\rho}\big\}.\) **Lemma 4.7** (Bounded-atom correction)**.** _Fix_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\)_. The following holds for all sufficiently large M. Let_ \(L\in\{1,\dots,M\}\) _and let_ \((X_1,\dots,X_L)\in\mathcal{S}_{L-1}(N,M)\)_, with Xk_=(_ak,bk_) _and empirical measure_ \(\mu=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k=1}^L\delta_{X_k}\)_. Then there exists an index k⋆ with_ (4.16) \(2\le b_{k_\star}\le a_{k_\star}.\) _Define a modified tuple_ \(\big(X'_1,\dots,X'_L\big)\) _by setting_ \(X'_{k_\star}:=\big(a_{k_\star}-1,b_{k_\star}-1\big);X'_k:=X_k\text{\textit{for}}k\neq k_\star,\) _and let_ \(\widehat{\mu}\) _be its empirical measure. Then_ \(\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[a]=\frac{N}{L};\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[b]=\frac{M}{L}.\) _Moreover, writing_ \(K_M:=\frac{(N+1)(N+2)}{2}\) _for the alphabet size, we have_ (4.17) \(\big|H(\widehat{\mu})-H(\mu)\big|\le\frac{1}{L}log(K_M-1)+h\left(1/L\right),\) _and_ (4.18) \(\big|\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[logw]-\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw]\big|\le\frac{1}{L}max_{2\le b\le a\le N+1}\big|logw(a,b)-logw(a-1,b-1)\big|.\) _In particular, uniformly over_ \(L\in\{1,\dots,M\}\)_, as_ \(M\rightarrow\infty\), (4.19) \(\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\widehat{\mu})+\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[logw]\big)=\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\mu)+\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw]\big)+o(1).\) _Proof._ The existence of an atom satisfying (4.16) follows since \(L\le M\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^Lb_k=M+1.\) Replacing (_a,b_) by (_a_-1_,b_-1) decreases the total sums by (1,1), hence changes (_N_+1_,M_+1) to (_N,M_), giving the mean identities. For (4.17), note that \(\mu\) and \(\widehat{\mu}\) are supported on an alphabet of size \(\le K_M\) and differ in total variation by at most 1_/L_ (one count is moved from one symbol to another), so the explicit Fannes-Audenaert bound gives the stated inequality. Since only one atom is changed, (4.18) is immediate. Finally, using _KM=O(M_2), \(max_{2\le b\le a\le N+1}\big|logw(a,b)-logw(a-1,b-1)\big|=O(logM),\) and \(h(1/L)\checkmark(logL)/L\), we obtain \(\frac{L}{N}\big|H(\widehat{\mu})-H(\mu)\big|\le\frac{1}{N}log(K_M-1)+\frac{L}{N}h(1/L)=o(1),\)
\(\frac{L}{N}\big|\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[logw]-\mathbb{E}_\mu[logw]\big|\le\frac{1}{N}max_{2\le b\le a\le N+1}\big|logw(a,b)-logw(a-1,b-1)\big|=o(1),\) which yields (4.19). □

<tbc>**Theorem 4.8** (Variational formula for <o>_Z_</o>)**.** _Fix_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) _and define_<tbc>

\(\mathsf{R}(\alpha):=sup_{\rho\in(0,1)}\alpha\rho\Phi(\rho).\)

<tbc>_Then we have_

(4.20) \(lim_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}log\overline{Z}=\mathsf{R}(\alpha).\)

_Proof._ We prove matching lower and upper bounds.

_Lower bound._ Fix \(\rho\in(0,1)\) and \(\eta>0\), and choose \(\nu\) with finite support such that \(\mathbb{E}_\nu[a]=1/(\alpha\rho)\), \(\mathbb{E}_\nu[b]=1/\rho\) and \(H(\nu)+\mathbb{E}_\nu[logw]\ge\Phi(\rho)-\eta\). Let \(D=\mathsf{supp}(\nu)\). For each large _M_, set \(L:=\lfloor\rho M\rfloor\) and choose integers \(n_x\ge 0\) for \(x\in D\) with \(\sum_{x\in D}n_x=L\) and

(4.21) \(|n_x/L-\nu(x)|\le|D|/L.\)

Let \(\mu_M^{(0)}\in\mathcal{M}_L\) be the corresponding empirical measure. Then as \(M\rightarrow\infty\),<tbc>

\(H(\mu_M^{(0)})\rightarrow H(\nu);\mathbb{E}_{\mu_M^{(0)}}[logw]\rightarrow\mathbb{E}_\nu[logw].\)

<tbc>The mean constraints for \(\overline{Z^{\le M}}\) require \(\mathbb{E}_\mu[a]=\frac{N+1}{L}\) and \(\mathbb{E}_\mu[b]=\frac{M+1}{L}\) , whereas \(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_M^{(0)}}[a]=\frac{A_0}{L}\) and \(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_M^{(0)}}[b]=\frac{B_0}{L}\) with

\(A_0=\sum_{x\in D}n_xa(x);B_0=\sum_{x\in D}n_xb(x).\)

Since \(\mu_M^{(0)}\rightarrow\nu\), we have _A_<sub>0</sub>=_N+O_(1) and _B_<sub>0</sub>=_M+O_(1). Here, the _O_(1) terms follow from (4.21).

We now adjust \(\mu_M^{(0)}\) into a new empirical measure \(\mu_M^{(1)}\in\mathcal{M}_L\) satisfying the _exact_ constraints by chang ing only _O_(1) atoms. We reserve a bounded buffer of the three symbols<tbc>

\(x_0:=(1,1),x_1:=(2,1),x_2:=(2,2),\text{for which}logw(x_i)=0.\)

<tbc>More precisely, choose a fixed constant _C_ large enough that \(C>|\Delta a|+|\Delta b|\) for all sufficiently large _M_, where<tbc>

\((\Delta a,\Delta b):=(N+1-A_0,M+1-B_0)\in\mathbb{Z}^2.\)

<tbc>When constructing the counts _n<sub>x</sub>_ above, we instead require \(\sum_{x\in D}n_x=L-3C\), and then adjoin _C_ copies each of _x_<sub>0</sub>_,x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>. This changes only _O_(1) atoms, so still \(\mu_M^{(0)}\rightarrow\nu\), and hence still _A_<sub>0</sub>=_N+O_(1) and _B_<sub>0</sub>=_M+O_(1). Now we can increase (_A_<sub>0</sub>_,B_<sub>0</sub>) by (1,0) (resp. (1,1)) by replacing one copy of _x_<sub>0</sub> by _x_<sub>1</sub> (resp. _x_<sub>2</sub>), and decrease them by reversing these moves; performing _O_(1) such moves yields exact means. Since only _O_(1) atoms are changed and log_w(x<sub>i</sub>_)=0, we still have<tbc>

\(H(\mu_M^{(1)})=H(\mu_M^{(0)})+o(1);\mathbb{E}_{\mu_M^{(1)}}[logw]=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_M^{(0)}}[logw]+o(1).\)

<tbc>Therefore,<tbc>

\(H(\mu_M^{(1)})+\mathbb{E}_{\mu_M^{(1)}}[logw]\ge\Phi(\rho)-\eta+o(1).\)

<tbc>Applying (4.14) to the admissible pair \((L,\mu_M^{(1)})\) gives<tbc>

\(liminf_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}log\overline{Z^{\le M}}\ge liminf_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\mu_M^{(1)})+\mathbb{E}_{\mu_M^{(1)}}[logw]\big)\ge\alpha\rho(\Phi(\rho)-\eta).\)

<tbc>Since \(\overline{Z}\ge\overline{Z^{\le M}}\), it follows that

\(liminf_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}log\overline{Z}\ge\alpha\rho(\Phi(\rho)-\eta).\)

Let \(\eta\downarrow 0\) and take the supremum over \(\rho\in(0,1)\) to obtain (4.22) \(\mathrm{liminf}_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\overline{Z}\ge\mathsf{R}(\alpha).\) _Upper bound._ Write \(\overline{Z}=\overline{Z^{\le M}}+\overline{Z^{(M+1)}},\) where \(\overline{Z^{(M+1)}}:=\sum_{(X_1,\dots,X_{M+1})\in\mathcal{S}_M(N,M)}\prod_{k=1}^{M+1}w(X_k).\) By (4.14), there exists \((L,\mu)\in\mathcal{I}_M\) such that \(\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\overline{Z^{\le M}}\le\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\mu)+\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathrm{log}w]\big)+o(1).\) Set \(\rho:=L/M\in(0,1]\). Since \(L\le M\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^Lb_k=M+1\), there exists an atom with \(b\ge 2\), so Lemma 4.7 applies. Thus there is \(\widehat{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}_L\) with \(\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[a]=\frac{N}{L}=\frac{1}{\alpha\rho},\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[b]=\frac{M}{L}=\frac{1}{\rho},\) and, by (4.19), \(\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\widehat{\mu})+\mathbb{E}_\widehat{\mu}[\mathrm{log}w]\big)=\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\mu)+\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathrm{log}w]\big)+o(1).\) Since \(\widehat{\mu}\) is finitely supported, it is admissible in the definition of \(\Phi(\rho)\), hence \(\frac{L}{N}\big(H(\mu)+\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathrm{log}w]\big)\le\alpha\rho\Phi(\rho)+o(1)\le\mathsf{R}(\alpha)+o(1).\) Therefore (4.23) \(\mathrm{limsup}_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\overline{Z^{\le M}}\le\mathsf{R}(\alpha).\) It remains to control _Z_(_M_+1). If \((X_1,\dots,X_{M+1})\in\mathcal{S}_M(N,M)\), then necessarily _bk_=1 for every _k_, since each \(b_k\ge 1\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^{M+1}b_k=M+1\). Hence _w(Xk_)=_w(ak,_1)=1 for all _k_, and \(\overline{Z^{(M+1)}}=\big|\{(a_1,\dots,a_{M+1})\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}^{M+1}:a_1+\cdots+a_{M+1}=N+1\}\big|=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{M}.\) Therefore (4.24) \(\mathrm{lim}_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\overline{Z^{(M+1)}}=h(\alpha).\) To compare this with \(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)\), fix \(\rho\in(1/2,1)\) and set \(\delta_\rho:=\rho^{-1}-1\). Let \(B_\rho\in\{1,2\}\) satisfy \(\mathbb{P}(B_\rho=2)=\delta_\rho;\)
\(\mathbb{P}(B_\rho=1)=1-\delta_\rho,\) so that \(\mathbb{E}[B_\rho]=1/\rho\). Let \(C_\rho\) be a geometric random variable on {0,1,2_,..._} with mean \(m_\rho:=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\rho},\) and independent of \(B_\rho\), and define \(A_\rho:=B_\rho+C_\rho\). Then \(A_\rho\ge B_\rho\) almost surely and \(\mathbb{E}[A_\rho]=\mathbb{E}[B_\rho]+\mathbb{E}[C_\rho]=\frac{1}{\rho}+\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\rho}=\frac{1}{\alpha\rho};\)

\(\mathbb{E}[B_\rho]=\frac{1}{\rho}.\)

<tbc>By truncating \(C_\rho\) and adjusting the top atom, we may approximate the law of \((A_\rho,B_\rho)\) by finitely supported admissible laws with the same moments and entropy arbitrarily close to \(H(A_\rho,B_\rho)\). Since \(w(a,b)\ge 1\), it follows that<tbc>

\(\Phi(\rho)\ge H(A_\rho,B_\rho)=H(B_\rho)+H(C_\rho).\)

<tbc>Now \(H(B_\rho)\rightarrow 0\) as \(\rho\uparrow 1\), while<tbc>

\(H(C_\rho)=\big(m_\rho+1\big)h\big(\frac{1}{m_\rho+1}\big)\longrightarrow\frac{1}{\alpha}h(\alpha)\)

<tbc>as \(\rho\uparrow 1\). Therefore<tbc>

\(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=sup_{\rho\in(0,1)}\alpha\rho\Phi(\rho)\ge limsup_{\rho\uparrow 1}\alpha\rho\big(H(B_\rho)+H(C_\rho)\big)=h(\alpha).\)

<tbc>Together with (4.24), this yields

(4.25) \(limsup_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}log\overline{Z^{(M+1)}}\le\mathsf{R}(\alpha).\)

Finally, using \(\overline{Z}=\overline{Z^{\le M}}+\overline{Z^{(M+1)}}\) and combining (4.22), (4.23), and (4.25), we conclude that

\(lim_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}log\overline{Z}=\mathsf{R}(\alpha),\)

which is (4.20). □

## 4.6. Solving the variational problem.

By Theorem 4.8, it remains to evaluate the supremum

\(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=sup_{\rho\in(0,1)}\alpha\rho\Phi(\rho),\)

where \(\Phi(\rho)\) was defined in (4.15). We solve this double optimisation (over \(\nu\) and over \(\rho\)) via Lagrange multipliers in four steps: first the inner problem for fixed \(\rho\), then a closed-form evaluation of the partition function, then the outer problem in \(\rho\), and finally the resulting algebraic system.

**Lemma 4.9** (Exponential family optimizer)**.** _Fix_ \(\rho\in(0,1)\)_. The supremum defining_ \(\Phi(\rho)\) _is attained by a unique probability measure_ \(\nu^*\) _of the form_

(4.26) \(\nu^*(a,b)=\frac{w(a,b)x^ay^b}{Z(x,y)},a\ge 1,1\le b\le a,\)

_where x,y\>_0 _are the unique positive solutions of the moment equations_ \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[a]=1/(\alpha\rho)\) _and_ \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[b]=1/\rho\)_, and_<tbc>

\(Z(x,y):=\sum_{a\ge 1}\sum_{b=1}^a\genfrac(){pt}{2}{a-1}{b-1}^2x^ay^b\)

<tbc>_is the partition function. The optimal value is_

(4.27) \(\Phi(\rho)=logZ(x,y)-\frac{1}{\alpha\rho}logx-\frac{1}{\rho}logy.\)

_Proof._ We first solve the inner variational problem for fixed \(\rho\) by Lagrange multipliers over the space of probability measures satisfying the moment constraints, which identifies the optimizer \(\nu^*\) and shows that it has the exponential family form (4.26). The functional

\(\nu\mapsto H(\nu)+\mathbb{E}_\nu[logw]\)

is strictly concave on the convex set of probability measures satisfying the moment constraints since _H_ is strictly concave and \(\mathbb{E}_\nu[\mathrm{log}w]\) is linear in \(\nu\). Furthermore, for any probability measure \(\nu\) satisfying these constraints, it follows from \(w(a,b)\le 4^a\) that \(\mathbb{E}_\nu[\mathrm{log}w]\le(\mathrm{log}4)\mathbb{E}_\nu[a]=(\mathrm{log}4)/(\alpha\rho)<\infty\) and, letting (_A,B_) be a random vector with law \(\nu\), \(H(\nu)=H(A,B)=H(A)+H(B|A)\le H(A)+\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}A\right]<\infty,\) so the evaluation of the functional at any such \(\nu\) is finite. Introducing Lagrange multipliers \(\lambda_0\) for the normalization constraint \(\sum_{a,b}\nu(a,b)=1\), \(\lambda_1\) for \(\mathbb{E}_\nu[a]=1/(\alpha\rho)\), and \(\lambda_2\) for \(\mathbb{E}_\nu[b]=1/\rho\), the first-order condition \(\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu(a,b)}\big[H(\nu)+\mathbb{E}_\nu[\mathrm{log}w]-\lambda_0\big(\sum\nu-1\big)-\lambda_1\big(\mathbb{E}_\nu[a]-1/(\alpha\rho)\big)-\lambda_2\big(\mathbb{E}_\nu[b]-1/\rho\big)\big]=0\) gives \(-\mathrm{log}\nu(a,b)-1+\mathrm{log}w(a,b)-\lambda_0-\lambda_1a-\lambda_2b=0\), hence \(\nu^*(a,b)=\frac{w(a,b)e^{-\lambda_1a}e^{-\lambda_2b}}{Z'},\) where \(Z'=e^{1+\lambda_0}\) ensures normalization. It can be shown that (1) the Lagrange multiplier equations admit a solution, i.e., corresponding values \(\lambda_0^*\), \(\lambda_1^*\), and \(\lambda_2^*\) for which the normalization and coordinate mean constraints are satisfied; (2) the corresponding measure \(\nu^*\) is the unique global maximizer of the objective functional. We do this in Appendix E. Letting \(\big(\lambda_1^*,\lambda_2^*\big)\) denote corresponding such values, setting the values \(x:=e^{-\lambda_1^*}\) and \(y:=e^{-\lambda_2^*}\) yields the form (4.26) with \(Z'=Z(x,y)\). To evaluate the optimal value, we substitute this optimizer into the objective and then approximate it by admissible measures. Since \(\mathrm{log}\nu^*(a,b)=\mathrm{log}w(a,b)+a\mathrm{log}x+b\mathrm{log}y-\mathrm{log}Z,\) substituting \(\nu^*\) into the functional to get \(H(\nu^*)+\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[\mathrm{log}w]\) yields that \(H(\nu^*)+\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[\mathrm{log}w]=-\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[\mathrm{log}\nu^*]+\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[\mathrm{log}w]=\mathrm{log}Z-(\mathrm{log}x)\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[a]-(\mathrm{log}y)\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[b],\) which is (4.27). Though \(\nu^*\) itself does not have finite support, we may approximate it via a sequence of finitely supported probability measures satisfying the moment constraints. Specifically, we define \(\mu_n(\cdot):=\nu^*\big(\cdot|E_n\big);E_n:=\left\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2:b\le a\le n\right\}.\) It directly follows from this construction that \(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_n}[a]\rightarrow\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[a]=1/(\alpha\rho);\mathbb{E}_{\mu_n}[b]\rightarrow\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[b]=1/\rho.\) Therefore, we may construct a sequence of probability measures \(\nu_n\) supported on the three tuples \((1,1),(2/\lfloor\alpha\rho\rfloor,1),(2/\lfloor\alpha\rho\rfloor,2/\lfloor\alpha\rho\rfloor)\) such that there exist values \(\epsilon_n\rightarrow 0\) for which the mixture probability measure \(\nu_n^*:=(1-\epsilon_n)\mu_n+\epsilon_n\nu_n\) satisfies the mean constraints \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_n}[a]=1/(\alpha\rho)\) and \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_n}[b]=1/\rho\). Then, we have that \(\big(H(\nu^*)+\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[\mathrm{log}w]\big)-\big(H(\nu_n)+\mathbb{E}_{\nu_n}[\mathrm{log}w]\big)=^\text{(E.3)}D_\text{KL}\big(\nu_n\big\|\nu^*\big)\)
\(\le(1-\epsilon_n)D_\text{KL}\big(\mu_n\big\|\nu^*\big)+\epsilon_nD_\text{KL}\big(\nu_n\big\|\nu^*\big)=-(1-\epsilon_n)\mathrm{log}\nu^*(E_n)+\epsilon_nD_\text{KL}\big(\nu_n\big\|\nu^*\big)\checkmark 1.\) This yields (4.27). □

<tbc>**Lemma 4.10** (Closed-form partition function)**.** _For all x,y\>_0 _with_ (1-_x-xy_)<sup>2</sup>_\>_4_x_<sup>2</sup>_y,_

(4.28) \(Z(x,y)=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{(1-x-xy)^2-4x^2y}}.\)

_Moreover,_ \(Z(x,y)=\infty\) _for all x,y\>_0 _that fail to satisfy this condition._

_Proof._ We begin by rewriting the partition function using a shift of indices together with Vandermonde’s identity. Shifting indices _m_:=_a_-1, _k_:=_b_-1 gives<tbc>

(4.29) \(Z(x,y)=xy\sum_{m=0}^\infty x^m\sum_{k=0}^m\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{k}^2y^k.\)

<tbc>For fixed _m_, the inner sum equals [_t<sup>m</sup>_](1+_t)<sup>m</sup>_(1+_yt)<sup>m</sup>_. Indeed,<tbc>

\((1+t)^m=\sum_i\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{i}t^i;(1+yt)^m=\sum_j\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{j}y^jt^j,\)

<tbc>and extracting the coefficient of _t<sup>m</sup>_ from their product gives<tbc>

\(\sum_{k=0}^m\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{k}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{m-k}y^k=\sum_k\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{k}^2y^k.\)

<tbc>Hence, we have that

(4.30) \(Z(x,y)=xy\sum_{m=0}^\infty[t^m]\left(x(1+t)(1+yt)\right)^m.\)

We now evaluate the resulting expression via residue computations. We write _f(t_):=_x_(1+_t_)(1+_yt_) and consider the "diagonal sum"<tbc>

\(\Sigma:=\sum_{m\ge 0}[t^m]f(t)^m.\)

<tbc>Since we have that<tbc>

\([t^m]f(t)^m=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint f(t)^mt^{-m-1}dt,\)

<tbc>summing the geometric series inside the integral yields<tbc>

\(\Sigma=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint\frac{dt}{t-f(t)},\)

<tbc>valid for a contour encircling the origin inside the region of convergence. The equation _t=f(t_), i.e., _t=x_(1+_t_)(1+_yt_), rearranges to

(4.31) \(Q(t):=xyt^2+(x+xy-1)t+x=0,\)

a quadratic in _t_ with discriminant

(4.32) \(D=D(x,y):=(1-x-xy)^2-4x^2y=\left(1-x(1+\sqrt{y})^2\right)\left(1-x(1-\sqrt{y})^2\right).\)

The two roots are

\(t_\pm=\frac{(1-x-xy)\pm\sqrt{D}}{2xy},\)

and _t_<sub>-</sub> is the small root enclosed by the contour. Since \(f'(t)=x(1+y)+2xyt\), we have

\(1-f'(t_-)=1-x(1+y)-2xyt_-=1-x-xy-\left[(1-x-xy)-\sqrt{D}\right]=\sqrt{D}.\)

<tbc>In particular, _t-f(t_) is increasing at \(t_-\neq 0\), so there exist values of _t_ for which |_f(t_)|_\<t_, and such a contour exists (e.g., via a circle with the appropriate radius). The residue at the simple pole _t_<sub>-</sub> of 1/(_t-f(t_)) is thus \(1/\sqrt{D}\), giving \(\Sigma=1/\sqrt{D}\), so \(Z=xy/\sqrt{D}\).

Finally, we show that once the discriminant condition fails, the series defining _Z(x,y_) diverges. It is clear that _Z(x,y_) is increasing in _x_. We fix _x,y\>_0 such that \(D(x,y)\le 0\). Taking \(0<x'<x\) small enough so that \(D(x',y)>0\) (which can be done, observed via the latter expression of (4.32)), it holds that

\(\frac{x'y}{\sqrt{D(x',y)}}\le Z(x,y).\)

Choosing \(x'\) arbitrarily close to \(x_y:=(1+\sqrt{y})^{-2}>0\), for which _D(x<sub>y</sub>,y_)=0, implies the result. □

**Proposition 4.11** (Unique interior maximizer and normalization)**.** _Let_<tbc>

\(g(\rho):=\alpha\rho\Phi(\rho),\rho\in(0,1).\)

<tbc>_Then g attains its maximum at a unique point_ \(\rho^*\in(0,1)\)_. If_ (_x_<sup>∗</sup>_,y_<sup>∗</sup>) _denotes the pair of parameters from Lemma 4.9 corresponding to_ \(\rho=\rho^*\)_, then_<tbc>

(4.33) \(Z(x^*,y^*)=1,\)

<tbc>_and consequently_

(4.34) \(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=-\mathrm{log}x^*-\alpha\mathrm{log}y^*.\)

_Proof._ For each \(\rho\in(0,1)\), let \(x=x(\rho)\) and \(y=y(\rho)\) be the unique positive parameters given by Lemma 4.9. By (4.27),

(4.35) \(g(\rho)=\alpha\rho\mathrm{log}Z(x,y)-\mathrm{log}x-\alpha\mathrm{log}y.\)

We first compute \(g'(\rho)\). The Lagrange multipliers for the inner problem are<tbc>

\(\alpha_1=-\mathrm{log}x\text{and}\alpha_2=-\mathrm{log}y,\)

<tbc>corresponding respectively to the constraints<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[a]=\frac{1}{\alpha\rho},\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[b]=\frac{1}{\rho}.\)

<tbc>By the envelope theorem,<tbc>

\(\frac{d\Phi}{d\rho}=\alpha_1\frac{d(1/(\alpha\rho))}{d\rho}+\alpha_2\frac{d(1/\rho)}{d\rho}=\frac{\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{log}x+\mathrm{log}y}{\rho^2}.\)

<tbc>Therefore,

(4.36) \(g'(\rho)=\alpha\Phi(\rho)+\alpha\rho\Phi'(\rho)=\alpha\big[\mathrm{log}Z-\frac{\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{log}x+\mathrm{log}y}{\rho}\big]+\alpha\frac{\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathrm{log}x+\mathrm{log}y}{\rho}=\alpha\mathrm{log}Z(x(\rho),y(\rho)).\)

Next we compute \(x(\rho),y(\rho)\), and \(Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))\) explicitly. By Lemma 4.10,<tbc>

\(Z(x,y)=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{D(x,y)}},D(x,y):=(1-x-xy)^2-4x^2y.\)

<tbc>Hence<tbc>

\(\mathrm{log}Z(x,y)=\mathrm{log}x+\mathrm{log}y-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{log}D(x,y).\)

<tbc>On the other hand, by the exponential family form of \(\nu^*\), we have

\(\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[a]=x\partial_x\mathrm{log}Z(x,y),\mathbb{E}_{\nu^*}[b]=y\partial_y\mathrm{log}Z(x,y).\)

<tbc>A direct computation gives<tbc>

\(x\partial_xlogZ(x,y)=\frac{1-x-xy}{D(x,y)},y\partial_ylogZ(x,y)=\frac{1-2x-xy+x^2(1-y)}{D(x,y)}.\)

<tbc>Therefore the moment constraints are equivalent to<tbc>

(4.37) \(\frac{1-x-xy}{D(x,y)}=\frac{1}{\alpha\rho},\)

<tbc>and

(4.38) \(\frac{1-2x-xy+x^2(1-y)}{D(x,y)}=\frac{1}{\rho}.\)

Solving (4.37)-(4.38) yields

(4.39) \(x(\rho)=\frac{(1-\alpha)(2-2\alpha+\alpha\rho)}{2-\alpha\rho},\)

and

(4.40) \(y(\rho)=\frac{\alpha^2(2-\rho)(1-\rho)}{(1-\alpha)(2-2\alpha+\alpha\rho)}.\)

Substituting (4.39)-(4.40) into the closed form for _Z_ gives<tbc>

(4.41) \(Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))=\frac{\alpha(1-\rho)\sqrt{2-\rho}}{\sqrt{\rho}\sqrt{(2-\alpha\rho)(2-2\alpha+\alpha\rho)}}.\)

<tbc>In particular,<tbc>

\(Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))\longrightarrow\infty\text{as}\rho\downarrow 0,\)

<tbc>and<tbc>

\(Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))\longrightarrow 0\text{as}\rho\uparrow 1.\)

<tbc>Moreover, \(Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))=1\) is equivalent, after squaring (4.41), to

(4.42) \(2\alpha^2\rho^2+(4\alpha-5\alpha^2-4)\rho+2\alpha^2=0.\)

The polynomial on the left-hand side of (4.42) has value \(2\alpha^2>0\) at \(\rho=0\) and value<tbc>

\(2\alpha^2+(4\alpha-5\alpha^2-4)+2\alpha^2=4\alpha-\alpha^2-4=-(2-\alpha)^2<0\)

<tbc>at \(\rho=1\). Hence it has at least one root in (0,1). Since its constant term equals its leading coefficient, the product of its roots is 1, so it can have at most one root in (0,1). Therefore there is a unique \(\rho^*\in(0,1)\) such that<tbc>

\(Z(x(\rho^*),y(\rho^*))=1.\)

<tbc>Because \(Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))\) is continuous, the uniqueness of \(\rho^*\) and the above boundary limits imply<tbc>

\(Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))>1\text{for}0<\rho<\rho^*,Z(x(\rho),y(\rho))<1\text{for}\rho^*<\rho<1.\)

<tbc>By (4.36), it follows that

\(g'(\rho)>0\text{for}0<\rho<\rho^*,g'(\rho)<0\text{for}\rho^*<\rho<1.\)

Thus _g_ is strictly increasing on \((0,\rho^*)\) and strictly decreasing on \((\rho^*,1)\), so _g_ attains its maximum uniquely at \(\rho^*\in(0,1)\).

Finally, setting \((x^*,y^*):=(x(\rho^*),y(\rho^*))\), we have proved (4.33). Plugging this into (4.35) gives

\(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=g(\rho^*)=-logx^*-\alpha logy^*,\)

which is (4.34). □

<tbc>**Proposition 4.12** (Explicit solution of the algebraic system)**.** _Writing_ \(c=1/\alpha\) _for algebraic convenience, for c\>_1 _(equivalently_ \(\alpha<1\)_), the system Z(x,y_)=1 _together with the stationarity condition from Proposition 4.11 has a unique solution_ \((x,y)\in(0,1)\times(0,\infty)\) _given by_ \(x=x_\alpha\) _and_ \(y=y_\alpha\) _as defined in Theorem 1.3._

_Proof._ By Lemma 4.10, _Z(x,y_)=1 is equivalent to<tbc>

\(xy=\sqrt{(1-x-xy)^2-4x^2y}.\)

<tbc>Squaring both sides yields<tbc>

\(x^2y^2=(1-x-xy)^2-4x^2y.\)

<tbc>Expanding the right-hand side and cancelling _x_<sup>2</sup>_y_<sup>2</sup> yields

(I) \(x^2(1-2y)-2x(1+y)+1=0,\)

which can be solved for _y_ as \(y=(1-x)^2/\big[2x(1+x)\big].\)

On the surface _Z_=1, the optimality of \(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=-\mathrm{log}x-\alpha\mathrm{log}y\) requires stationarity with respect to (_x,y_) constrained to (I). Writing<tbc>

\(Q(x,y):=x^2(1-2y)-2x(1+y)+1,\)

<tbc>the Lagrange condition \(\nabla[-\mathrm{log}x-\alpha\mathrm{log}y]=\lambda\nabla Q\) gives (after dividing the two components)

(II) \(\frac{(1+y)-x(1-2y)}{y(x+1)}=c.\)

This can be solved for _y_ as \(y=(1-x)/\big[(c-1)+(c-2)x\big].\)

Equating the two expressions for _y_ from (I) and (II) (and dividing by \(1-x\neq 0\) for _c\>_1) gives<tbc>

\(\frac{1-x}{2x(1+x)}=\frac{1}{(c-1)+(c-2)x}.\)

<tbc>Cross-multiplying: \((1-x)\big[(c-1)+(c-2)x\big]=2x(1+x)\), which expands and simplifies to the quadratic

(4.43) \(cx^2+3x-(c-1)=0.\)

By the quadratic formula, the unique positive root is<tbc>

\(x=\frac{-3+\sqrt{9+4c(c-1)}}{2c}=\frac{-3+\sqrt{4c^2-4c+9}}{2c}.\)

<tbc>Since \(\sqrt{4c^2-4c+9}=c\sqrt{9c^{-2}-4c^{-1}+4}=c\Delta(c)\), we obtain \(x=\big(\Delta(c)-3c^{-1}\big)/2=x_c\). Substituting back into _y_=(1-_x_)<sup>2</sup>/\[2_x_(1+_x_)\] and using \(\Delta-3/c=2x_c\) (hence \(3/c+2-\Delta=2(1-x_c)\) and \(2+\Delta-3/c=2(1+x_c)\)), we get

\(y_c=\frac{4(1-x_c)^2}{2\cdot 2x_c\cdot 2(1+x_c)}=\frac{(3c^{-1}+2-\Delta(c))^2}{2(\Delta(c)-3c^{-1})(2+\Delta(c)-3c^{-1})},\)

matching the definition in Theorem 1.3. Since \(\sqrt{4c^2-4c+9}>3\) for _c\>_1, we have _x<sub>c</sub>\>_0, and since 0_\<x<sub>c</sub>\<_1 we have _y<sub>c</sub>\>_0. □

_Proof of Theorem 1.3._ By Theorem 4.8, \(\mathrm{lim}_{M\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\overline{Z}=\mathsf{R}(\alpha)\). By Propositions 4.11 and 4.12,

\(\mathsf{R}(\alpha)=-\mathrm{log}x_\alpha-\alpha\mathrm{log}y_\alpha,\)

which gives (4.1). By the discussion at the beginning of Section 4, this proves Theorem 1.3. □

## 5. Open Problems

We conclude the paper with several suggestions for future research.

## 5.1. A conjectural formula for \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\).

We recall that our main motivation in this paper is the identity (1.3), which reduces the problem of computing the uniform capacity of the deletion channel to understanding the planted quenched free energy \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\) with \(\alpha=1-p\). While Theorem 1.3 gives an exact formula for the corresponding annealed free energy, the problem of computing the quenched free energy is likely to be much more challenging. In particular, as suggested by Figure 1, we expect the following analogue of Theorem 1.1 to hold. In words, Conjecture 5.1 states that the Jensen gap corresponding to the planted Random Subsequence Model is also always nontrivial, just as it was for the null model.

**Conjecture 5.1.** _It holds for any_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) _that_

\(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)<f_\mathrm{pl}^\mathrm{ann}(\alpha).\)

Given the suspected difficulty of exactly determining the value \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\), a first step is to at least aim for a convincing conjectural description of this quantity. We illustrate why even non-rigorously deriving such a prediction for this free energy is challenging, by considering two very natural approaches to this problem and discussing the key obstructions that each approach encounters.

**The replica method.** In light of Theorem 1.3, perhaps the most natural candidate method for deriving a prediction is with a replica calculation. Let \(Z=Z_{X^\prime,Y}\) be under the null law on independent uniform strings \(X'\in\{0,1\}^N\) and \(Y\in\{0,1\}^M\). By Nishimori’s identity, if (_X,Y_) are distributed according to the planted law, we have<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{log}Z_{X,Y}]=\left.\frac{\mathbb{E}[Z\mathrm{log}Z]}{\mathbb{E}[Z]}=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial q}\mathrm{log}\mathbb{E}[Z^q]\right|_{q=1}.\)

<tbc>Thus, a replica computation for \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\) would begin by studying<tbc>

\(\Phi_r(\alpha):=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{log}\mathbb{E}[Z^r]\text{for integers}r\ge 1,\)

<tbc>and then seeking (non-rigorous) continuation in the replica number. The difficulty is that the integer moments already appear to be highly nontrivial. Indeed, for \(r\in\mathbb{N}\),

(5.1) \(\mathbb{E}[Z^r]=\sum_{\sigma^1,\dots,\sigma^r\in\Sigma_{N,M}}\mathbb{P}\left(X_{\sigma^1}=\cdots=X_{\sigma^r}=Y\right).\)

For a fixed _r_-tuple \(\left(\sigma^1,\dots,\sigma^r\right)\), this probability depends on the full structure of the bipartite union graph \(G=G\left(\sigma^1,\dots,\sigma^r\right)\) on vertex set \([M]\sqcup[N]\) obtained by connecting each \(j\in[M]\) to those \(\sigma^a(j)\in[N]\) used by the replicas for \(a\in[r]\). More precisely, we have that

\(\mathbb{P}\left(X_{\sigma^1}=\cdots=X_{\sigma^r}=Y\right)=2^{\kappa(G)-(M+N)},\)

where \(\kappa(G)\) is the number of connected components of _G_. Thus the contribution of a replica configuration is not determined merely by a pairwise overlap matrix on configurations in \(\Sigma\) for values \(r\ge 3\), as was the case in Section 4, which is equivalent to the _r_=2 case of the above computation. Starting at _r_=3, tuples with the same pairwise overlap statistics can have different union graph topology and hence different weights in (5.1). In particular, there does not seem to be a candidate finite-dimensional order parameter in terms of which the replica computation can be closed.

**The cavity method.** Another appealing route is via the cavity method. Starting from the recursion of (1.4) applied to the entire strings \((X,Y)\in\{0,1\}^N\times\{0,1\}^M\), i.e.,<tbc>

\(Z_{N,M}=\unknown\{X_N=Y_M\}Z_{N-1,M-1}+Z_{N-1,M},\)

<tbc>we can eventually obtain

\(\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}Z_{N,M}\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}Z_{N-1,M}\right]=-\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}\langle\sigma_1\neq 1\rangle_{N,M}\right],\)
