Assuming that the cavity field \(\langle\sigma_1\neq 1\rangle_{N,M}\) converges in law to a random variable \(P(\alpha)\) as \(N,M\rightarrow\infty\) with \(M/N=\alpha\), then that would imply

\(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)=-\int_0^{1-\alpha}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}P\big(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+x}\big)\right]dx.\)

Thus, the challenge in this approach is to derive a plausible closed-form description for the limit law of the cavity field \(P(\alpha)\). In the context of mean-field spin glasses, this is often obtained as a consequence of a self-consistency relation. We have not been able to find such a relation.

### 5.2. Mean-field versus rank-one free energies.

The natural mean-field version of the null Random Subsequence Model is where one replaces the "rank one" matrix \(B_{ij}=\unknown\{X_i=Y_j\}\) by a matrix with i.i.d. entries drawn from a common distribution D (see Section 1.1.3). The choice of D closest to the true Random Subsequence Model is D=Unif{0,1}, which has been studied under the name "Bernoulli Matching Model" in relation to the longest common subsequence problem \[Bou99; MN05\]. The case where D=Gamma(_a,b_) corresponds to the Strict-Weak lattice polymer \[CSS15\]. Let \(f^\mathrm{BMM}(\alpha)\) and \(f^\mathrm{SW}(a,b)(\alpha)\) denote their (quenched) free energies, respectively. To what extent do these quantities relate to or control the Random Subsequence Model’s free energy? We pose the following conjecture.

**Conjecture 5.2.** _For all_ \(\alpha\in[0,1]\)_, it holds that_

\(f_\mathrm{null}(\alpha)\le f^\mathrm{BMM}(\alpha)\le f^{\mathrm{SW}(1,1/2)}(\alpha).\)

We recall that the experience in the directed polymers literature suggests that only problems with special algebraic structure admit exact analytic solutions, which represents an important barrier to obtaining exact formulas for the free energy of the Random Subsequence Model. Moreover, while the solvable Strict-Weak Polymer Model is an analogue of the null Random Subsequence Model, as far as the authors are aware, no solvable analogue (in this sense) of the _planted_ Random Subsequence Model is known. Indeed, the planted structure already seems to break the requisite algebraic structure. The next open problem suggests such an analogue. We see this model as breaking the algebraic structure in the minimal way, and hence view it as a promising stepping stone towards the Random Subsequence Model.

**Problem 5.3.** _Let_ \(B\in\mathbb{R}_+^{N\times M}\) _have i.i.d._ Gamma(_a,b_) _entries. Independently, sample_ \(\sigma^*\sim\Sigma_{NM}\)_, and for every j_=1_,...,M, over-write_ \(B_{\sigma(j),j}=1\)_. Let Z<sub>NM</sub> be the corresponding free energy obtained from_ (1.5)_, and define_

\(f_\mathrm{pl}^{\mathrm{SW}(a,b)}(\alpha)=\mathrm{lim}_{N,M\rightarrow\infty M/N=\alpha}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{log}Z_{NM}\right].\)

_Find an exact analytic formula for_ \(f_\mathrm{pl}^{\mathrm{SW}(a,b)}(\alpha)\).

### 5.3. Asymptotics in the likely deletion regime.

Corollary 1.2 establishes that the uniform capacity of the deletion channel is strictly positive for every _p\<_1. However, the explicit lower bound extracted from our argument in Theorem 3.13 is too small to capture the asymptotic behavior of \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\) as \(\alpha=1-p\rightarrow 0\). It remains open to determine the asymptotic order of magnitude of \(f_\mathrm{pl}(\alpha)\) as \(\alpha\rightarrow 0\), which would be very interesting.

## Appendix E. Addendum to the Proof of Lemma 4.9

We list some results on exponential families here that we invoke later.

**Theorem E.1** ([WJ08, Equation (3.28)])**.** _In an exponential family with discrete state space_ X _and sufficient statistic_ \(\phi(X)\)_, the mean parameter space_ M _admits the representation_

\(\mathcal{M}=\mathrm{conv}\left(\{\phi(x):x\in\mathcal{X}\}\right),\)

_where_ conv _denotes the convex hull operation._

**Theorem E.2** ([WJ08, Theorem 3.3])**.** _In a minimal exponential family with parameter space_ \(\Omega\)_, sufficient statistic_ \(\phi(X)\)_, and log-partition function A, the gradient map_ \(\nabla_\theta A\) _is onto_ \(\mathcal{M}^\circ\)_, the interior of the mean parameter space. Consequently, for each_ \(\mu\in\mathcal{M}^\circ\)_, there exists some_ \(\theta\in\theta(\mu)\in\Omega\) _such that_ \(\mathbb{E}_\theta[\phi(X)]=\mu\).

For \(\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\), defining (with the correspondence \(\theta_1=-\lambda_1\) and \(\theta_2=-\lambda_2\))<tbc>

\(A(\theta):=\mathrm{log}\left(\sum_{a,b}w(a,b)e^{\theta_1a+\theta_2b}\right)\)

<tbc>gives the log-partition function of the exponential family supported on \(\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}^2:1\le b\le a\}\) with mass function \(p_\theta(a,b)\) defined via

\(p_\theta(a,b)\propto w(a,b)e^{\theta_1a+\theta_2b}\Longrightarrow p_\theta(a,b)=w(a,b)e^{\langle\theta,(a,b)\rangle-A(\theta)}.\)

<tbc>As the sufficient statistic of this exponential family is (_a,b_), which is not contained in an affine line, the family is thus minimal. Additionally, since \(p_\theta\) has discrete support, it follows from Theorem E.1 that the mean parameter space is<tbc>

\(\mathcal{M}:=\left\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^2:1\le\beta\le\alpha\right\}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{M}^\circ=\left\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^2:1<\beta<\alpha\right\}.\)

<tbc>It follows from Lemma 4.10 (whose proof does not rely on the preceding Lemma 4.9) and (4.32) that<tbc>

\(\Omega:=\left\{(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2:A(\theta)<\infty\right\}=\left\{(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in(-\infty,0)^2:e^{\theta_1}(1+e^{\theta_2/2})^2<1\right\}.\)

<tbc>It readily follows from this description of \(\Omega\) that for any \(\gamma=(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\in\Omega\), there exists an open box \(I\subset\Omega\) such that \(\gamma\in I\) and uniformly over \(\theta\in I\),<tbc>

\(\sum_{a,b}\frac{\partial p_\theta(a,b)}{\partial\theta_1}=\sum_{a,b}a\cdot p_\gamma(a,b)<\infty;\sum_{a,b}\frac{\partial p_\theta(a,b)}{\partial\theta_2}=\sum_{a,b}b\cdot p_\gamma(a,b)\le\sum_{a,b}a\cdot p_\gamma(a,b)<\infty.\)

<tbc>It thus follows that this family satisfies, for all \(\theta\in\Omega\), that

(E.1) \(\nabla_\theta A(\theta)=\left(\mathbb{E}_\theta[a],\mathbb{E}_\theta[b]\right),\)

which we want to be equal to \((1/(\alpha\rho),1/\rho)\in\mathcal{M}^\circ\). Altogether, Theorem E.2 yields the existence of \((\theta_1^*,\theta_2^*)\) for which (E.1) is satisfied. Letting \(\left(\lambda_1^*,\lambda_2^*\right)=(-\theta_1^*,-\theta_2^*)\), we may then set \(\lambda_0^*\) via<tbc>

\(e^{1+\lambda_0^*}=\sum_{a,b}w(a,b)e^{-\lambda_1^*a-\lambda_2^*b}.\)

<tbc>We conclude that this system of equations has a solution. We now let \(\nu^*\), _Z_<sup>∗</sup>, \(\lambda_1^*\), and \(\lambda_2^*\) denote the corresponding quantities for such a solution. It holds that

(E.2) \(\mathrm{log}\nu^*(a,b)=\mathrm{log}w(a,b)-\lambda_1^*a-\lambda_2^*b-\mathrm{log}Z^*.\)

For any probability measure \(\nu\), the objective functional may be expressed via

\(H(\nu)+\mathbb{E}_\nu\left[\mathrm{log}w\right]=-\sum_{a,b}\nu(a,b)\mathrm{log}\nu(a,b)+\sum_{a,b}\nu(a,b)\mathrm{log}w(a,b)=-\sum_{a,b}\nu(a,b)\mathrm{log}\nu(a,b)+\sum_{a,b}\nu(a,b)\mathrm{log}\nu^*+\sum_{a,b}\nu\lambda_1^*a+\sum\nu(a,b)\lambda_2^*b+\sum_{a,b}\nu(a,b)\mathrm{log}Z^*=-\sum_{a,b}\nu(a,b)\mathrm{log}\frac{\nu(a,b)}{\nu^*(a,b)}+\frac{c\lambda_1}{\rho}+\frac{\lambda_2}{\rho}+\mathrm{log}Z^*=\frac{c\lambda_1}{\rho}+\frac{\lambda_2}{\rho}+\mathrm{log}Z^*-D_\mathrm{KL}\left(\nu\left\|\nu^*\right\right\rangle\) (E.3)

where the first equality in the third line is due to the normalization and mean constraints applied to the solution. Since \(D_\mathrm{KL}\left(\nu\left\|\nu^*\right\rangle\ge 0\), we conclude that \(\nu^*\) is a global maximizer of the objective functional.
